item.title: EvoSeq: A Eukaryotic Sequence-Function Profiling Platform for AI-Guided Engineering of Genome-Editing Enzymes.
item.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping protein engineering, yet progress remains constrained by the limited availability of scalable, normalized sequence-activity datasets and experimental benchmarks. Reported here is Evolution by Sequencing (EvoSeq), a sequencing-based profiling platform for genome-editing enzymes that links each variant to a reporter sequence change, enabling activity and variant sequence to be quantified together by next-generation sequencing. Representative sequencing-assisted workflows either require separate functional assays or were performed in bacteria. EvoSeq performs sequence-activity profiling in eukaryotic yeast system with reduced background by up to 95-fold compared to bacterial system, positioning EvoSeq as a pooled eukaryotic alternative to workflows that require separate functional assays and to approaches demonstrated primarily in bacteria. Application to adenine base editor evolution identifies variants with 1.4-fold higher on-target activity at a HBG gene target and threefold lower off-target editing at PCSK9 after mRNA-lipid nanoparticle validation in HepG2 cells. An intron-embedded homologous-recombination recording strategy further enables direct evolution of the large Cas12i nuclease CasY7 and supports active learning, increasing the hit rate of model-nominated mutational windows compared with manual selection. EvoSeq therefore provides an experimental benchmarking method for AI-guided protein-design algorithms and AI-compatible sequence-activity profiling platform for engineering genome editors in eukaryotic cells.

item.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST.
item.abstract: Precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering. CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs)1,2 offer a promising solution by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration. Because of their exceptional targeting fidelity, type I-F3 CASTs have been a major research focus1, yet the structural basis of their RNA-guided DNA integration has remained unclear. Here, using cryo-electron microscopy, computational protein design and functional assays, we report the licensing mechanisms that control DNA integration activity of Vibrio cholerae CAST (VchCAST). Structural determination was enabled by zero-shot computational redesign of TnsA, which enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude without compromising specificity. The structure of the holo integration complex reveals the conformational licensing events that govern activation of the integration machinery at the on-target site. Multiple components (Cascade-TniQ, TnsC and TnsA-TnsB) undergo conformational changes upon assembly into the holo integration complex, and the catalytically competent state is stabilized only within the full assembly. Comparison with existing CAST integration complex structures reveals conserved architectural features, suggesting a common molecular basis for RNA-guided transposition across CASTs. Our findings establish a general mechanistic framework for RNA-guided DNA integration and demonstrate that protein design is a powerful strategy for engineering highly active CAST systems.

item.title: RNA manipulation for synthetic biology: from molecular tools to programmable cellular systems.
item.abstract: Beyond traditional transcriptional regulation, synthetic biology is increasingly turning its focus to the direct manipulation of RNA molecules, leveraging RNA stability, localization, translation, and processing to impose dynamic, reversible, and resource-efficient control over gene expression. This review presents a comprehensive overview of the evolving RNA manipulation toolkit, ranging from fundamental molecular tools to sophisticated and programmable cellular systems. We categorize existing strategies into two primary paradigms: RNA-centric approaches (e.g., synthetic riboregulators) and protein-coupled systems (e.g., RNA-binding proteins and CRISPR-Cas effectors). A central theme of this review is the integration of these tools with functional modules, such as translation control mechanisms, RNA modification enzymes, and synthetic biomolecular condensates, to construct higher-order cellular systems capable of precise spatiotemporal regulation. We discuss the significant potential of these programmable RNA systems in circuit design, metabolic engineering, and RNA modification. Additionally, we critically evaluate challenges related to specificity, orthogonality, and host compatibility, and propose future directions focused on multiplexed RNA circuit design, modular standardization, and the development of closed-loop control architectures. This review aims to highlight the emerging utility of RNA manipulation tools and their integration into synthetic biology frameworks.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems.
item.abstract: CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR-Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3-6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade-TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC-TnsB and TnsB-target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

item.title: Engineering live biotherapeutic products (eLBPs): modularization and systematic building strategies.
item.abstract: The continued advancement of synthetic biology and related technologies has reinvigorated traditional probiotic therapies. Researchers can customize the bacterial chassis to construct eLBPs on demand. These can perform a variety of functions, including sensing and processing of disease signals, in situ production or targeted delivery of drugs, and long-term treatment of chronic diseases. The performance of these functions depends on the precise cooperation between the modules and the rational design of the genetic circuit. However, the mechanisms of some microbial-host interactions remain unclear, and modular design approaches are lacking. These problems have largely hindered the further development of eLBPs. Here, we review the current state of development of eLBPs and the problems encountered, followed by possible solutions and potential future research directions. The engineering components in eLBPs are categorized as: sensor module, signal processing module, delivery module, containment module, and colonization module. The modular construction strategy can facilitate the design of eLBPs and expedite their deployment in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases. Finally, we describe the design process of eLBPs based on modularization strategies, discuss the differences between this approach and the traditional drug development process, and provide an outlook on the future development and potential problems associated with this technology.

item.title: [Intelligent enzyme engineering paradigm evolution and future toolkits].
item.abstract: Enzyme engineering is undergoing a profound paradigm shift from experience-driven approaches to a novel dual-driven framework integrating data and mechanism insights. Grounded in massive biological datasets, this paradigm deeply integrates computational biology, artificial intelligence (AI), and synthetic biology to establish an intelligent, end-to-end pipeline spanning discovery, design, and application. For enzyme mining, the synergistic application of sequence/structure-based evolutionary analysis, graph neural networks (GNNs), diffusion models, and ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) provides evolutionary and structural priors for identifying functional diversification branches, ancestral nodes, and potential functional sites, with the potential to improve the efficiency of novel enzyme discovery and experimental validation. In the engineering and optimization phase, AI models such as AlphaFold 3 and ESM3 profoundly empower rational design and directed evolution. By leveraging multimodal feature learning and intelligent library construction, these tools may partially alleviate data scarcity in mapping the "sequence-structure-function" relationships of novel enzymes. At the system integration level, synthetic biology underpinned by standardized biological part libraries, genetic design automation (GDA), and high-throughput experimental platforms drives enzyme applications from single-molecule optimization to systematic metabolic pathway regulation. This further provides an implementation basis for a learn-frontloaded learn-design-build-test (LDBT) workflow that integrates data learning and model prediction before experimental design and testing. Collectively, the deep intersection of evolutionary trajectory analysis, AI-driven predictive algorithms, and synthetic biology establishes a closed-loop workflow of "computational prediction-experimental validation-model iteration". This synergy comprehensively propels enzyme engineering into a new era of highly efficient and predictable bioengineering, laying a robust foundation for modern biomanufacturing and the green bioeconomy.

item.title: From molecular dynamics to generative design: Engineering enzymes for predictive, programmable, and sustainable biocatalysis.
item.abstract: Enzyme engineering is evolving from empirical mutation-screening toward predictive, AI-enabled biocatalyst design, offering new opportunities to overcome the interdependent tradeoffs governing catalytic efficiency, thermostability, substrate specificity, and process tolerance. This review critically examines advances in structure-guided redesign, active-site and loop engineering, conformational dynamics, allosteric-network modulation, and computational thermostabilization. It integrates insights from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, molecular dynamics, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics simulations to elucidate the structural and dynamic determinants of enzyme function. Particular attention is given to machine-learning-guided mutation prediction, protein language models, and generative protein design, highlighting their complementary roles in navigating sequence space and identifying functionally optimized variants. A central contribution is the integration of generative design with ensemble-based molecular dynamics as a conformational validation strategy, illustrated through an engineered cytochrome P450 case study. Industrial translation is critically assessed across pharmaceutical synthesis, CO2 valorization, biomass conversion, and biofuel production, distinguishing molecular-level performance gains from process-level sustainability, including enzyme manufacture, cofactor requirements, and downstream processing. Persistent barriers involving data quality, epistasis, model generalizability, experimental reproducibility, and scale-up are evaluated. Finally, a closed-loop framework integrating computational prediction, experimental validation, and process engineering is proposed to accelerate the development of robust, manufacturable, and sustainable industrial biocatalysts.

item.title: [Advances in ProteinMPNN-driven protein engineering].
item.abstract: Biomanufacturing is a key pathway for promoting the green transformation of conventional production methods. Its core bottleneck lies in the difficulty of natural enzymes to meet the requirements of industrial applications, necessitating the customized modification of enzyme molecules through protein engineering. Conventional semi-rational design is limited by a narrow sequence search space, heavy reliance on known structural information, and high experimental screening costs, which make it difficult to achieve precise design of industrial-grade enzyme molecules. In recent years, artificial intelligence-based protein design technologies represented by ProteinMPNN have made breakthrough progress and are driving a profound paradigm shift in protein engineering. This article systematically describes the technical principles, workflow, and methodological advantages of ProteinMPNN, compares it with Rosetta and other protein design models, and reviews the research progress of this technology in industrial enzyme engineering and biomanufacturing. On this basis, this article discusses current research hotspots and challenges in industrial application, and provides an outlook on future development directions and prospects for industrial implementation. It is expected to serve as a reference for fundamental research and industrial translation in synthetic biology and protein engineering.

item.title: [Advances in in vivo directed evolution systems for microorganisms].
item.abstract: Conventional microbial strain engineering predominantly relies on iterative cycles of in vitro mutagenesis and rational design, a paradigm often constrained by limited library throughput and the unpredictable nature of complex phenotypes. To overcome these bottlenecks, researchers have shifted focus to the intracellular environment, developing in vivo directed evolution technologies that generate genetic diversity and enable selection directly within the host, thereby drastically shortening evolutionary timescales and greatly increasing the number of accessible beneficial mutations. This review systematically summarizes representative technologies and advances in this field from the past decade, organized by their mutation introduction mechanisms. It covers strategies ranging from early recombination-mediated integration of oligonucleotides or error-prone PCR products (e.g., MAGE and TRMR) to continuous evolution systems based on error-prone DNA polymerases [e.g., phage-assisted continuous evolution (PACE) and OrthoRep]; from Ty1 retrotransposon-mediated mutagenesis to targeted deaminase-based tools (e.g., MutaT7 and base editors); and emerging platforms driven by error-prone RNA polymerases or the NHEJ repair pathway. These technologies each possess distinct characteristics in mutational spectrum, targeting precision, and host applicability, collectively exhibiting three major trends: the shift of mutagenesis from in vitro to autonomous in vivo processes, the transition of operational modes from serial manual cycles to automated continuous processes, and the expanding of host range toward industrially relevant microorganisms. Building on these trends, the synergistic advancement of mutagenesis tools and screening methods promises to overcome the bottleneck of generating diversity without the tools for screening, propelling in vivo directed evolution toward a universal technology platform applicable to a broad range of chassis organisms and complex phenotypes. This review systematically summarizes the principles, advantages, and limitations of various technologies, discusses future directions for the synergistic advancement of mutagenesis tools and screening methods, and provides guidance for researchers in selecting appropriate technologies based on specific evolutionary objectives, offering important insights for advancing in vivo directed evolution toward a universal technology platform.

item.title: [AI-driven design of regulatory parts for microbial chassis].
item.abstract: Synthetic biology aims to design, modify, or synthesize new biological parts, genetic networks, and metabolic pathways from the bottom up, and even to create artificial cells with specific functions, offering transformative solutions in medicine, chemical engineering, energy, and other fields. In constructing complex biological systems, the underlying biological parts serve as the core basic components. Conventional methods for obtaining parts rely mainly on mining and characterizing natural organisms, which are not only time-consuming and labor-intensive but also depend on lengthy empirical trial-and-error, making it difficult to meet diverse industrial demands. Using artificial intelligence (AI) to study parts enables the precise mining of implicit mapping relationships between massive biological sequences and their functions, thereby allowing efficient prediction of part expression levels and breaking through the constraints of natural species to design de novo high-activity parts that do not exist in nature. Building upon this, this paper systematically reviews the latest advances in the AI-assisted design of biological parts for microbial chassis. It first outlines the advantages of underlying AI algorithms in feature extraction and generation of biological sequences. Then, it details the specific applications and breakthroughs of AI technologies in engineering and de novo designing two core categories-transcriptional regulatory parts and translational regulatory parts-across different chassis cells. Finally, the article discusses the current challenges, such as data sparsity and weak cross-species generalization, in AI design and provides an outlook on a new blueprint for efficient part development that integrates physics-based models, large language models, and fully automated laboratories in the future. This review provides theoretical references for accelerating the rational design of biological parts and advancing the intelligent and industrial development of synthetic biology.

item.title: Design of High-Affinity Mini-Protein Drug Conjugates Targeting TROP2.
item.abstract: Accurate and effective treatment of solid tumors has long been a core issue in cancer therapy. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent a crucial breakthrough in precision oncology. Traditional ADCs rely on monoclonal antibodies generated through animal immunization, followed by screening, sequencing, and recombinant expressiona process that is experimentally complex and costly. In this study, we employed deep learning-based computational design methods to design mini-protein binders targeting the tumor-associated antigen TROP2. The designed TROP2 mini-protein binder exhibited high specificity and thermal stability. The binding affinity was optimized from 40.4 nM to 628 pM through partial diffusion. On this basis, we engineered the mini-protein binder by conjugating it with the microtubule inhibitor VcMMAE, thereby constructing mini-protein drug conjugates (MPDCs) that can specifically target and kill TROP2-positive tumor cells. A comprehensive assessment of the anti-tumor efficacy of these MPDCs was performed using cancer cell lines, organoid models, and mouse xenograft models.

item.title: Manufacturing of Protein-Based Biomaterials Coupling Cell-Free Protein Synthesis with Protein Immobilization.
item.abstract: Manufacturing of protein-based biomaterials is gaining momentum in biomedical applications. In this chapter, we describe the procedures to create a versatile platform for the one-pot fabrication of different types of protein-based biomaterials by coupling the in vitro protein synthesis with the protein immobilization on solid materials in one pot. To this aim, a set of plasmids and a battery of solid materials must be developed to guarantee the selective immobilization of the nascent protein on the surfaces, giving rise to functional biomaterials. This methodology also allows functionalizing materials with two or more proteins to increase the biomaterial's functionalities. Herein, this technology only requires the genomic information encoding the target protein, the desired solid material, and the cell-free extract containing the protein synthesis machinery. The cooperative action of all these elements turns this portable technology into an innovative strategy for prototyping the fabrication of biomaterials and shortening their processing time.

item.title: Design and Evolution of an Orthogonal HaloTag for Multiplexed Labeling in Cells.
item.abstract: The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag's superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.

item.title: Modeling Protein Evolution with Generative Models: From Extant Sequence Data to Evolutionary Dynamics.
item.abstract: Protein sequences carry a record of evolutionary history shaped by mutation, selection, drift, and epistasis. Recent generative models trained on homologous sequence families offer a new way to read this record: they define probabilistic landscapes that score sequences, generate viable variants, and capture constraints that are difficult to measure experimentally. In this review, we discuss how such landscapes can be used not only for protein design or mutation-effect prediction, but also for modeling evolutionary dynamics. We focus particularly on Direct Coupling Analysis as an interpretable and experimentally validated framework, while placing it in the broader context of generative sequence modeling. We first describe how generative sequence landscapes are inferred and assessed, then review how they can be coupled to population-genetic or substitution-model dynamics to simulate protein evolution across experimental and phylogenetic timescales. Applications include viral evolution, laboratory drift experiments, historical contingency, entrenchment, epistatic drift over time, and long-term sequence-space exploration. We conclude by discussing open challenges, including score-fitness calibration, phylogenetic structure, codon-level mutation biases, indels, and the integration of experimental data.

item.title: Native Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteoform Explicit Metrics System (PrEMS) Informs Structural Improvement of Artificial Photocyclase Enzymes.
item.abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful strategy for enzyme engineering and has successfully enabled unique stereoselective biosynthesis of high-value organic molecules. Enantiomeric excess (ee) remains the gold standard to assess the enzyme performance, but only reflects the final reaction outcome and provides limited mechanistic insights, leaving design efforts effectively a ″black box″, especially for multimeric proteins and heterogeneous systems. Here, we introduce a Proteoform Explicit Metrics System (PrEMS) that links protein point mutations and catalytic enantioselectivity via structural features measured by native mass spectrometry (native MS). Using 11 artificial photocyclase mutants, we demonstrate that single-point mutations can have a profound impact on protein structure, resulting in a highly convoluted effect on protein function not easily explainable by a single variable. We derived a multiple linear regression (MLR) model from the proteoform explicit native MS data based on the enzyme's oligomeric state, photosensitizer labeling efficiency, susceptibility to oxidation, and photodegradation half-life. PrEMS showed significantly higher correlation (adjusted R2 increases from 0.053 to 0.869) to the enzyme's enantioselectivity than the conventional physicochemical descriptors of the mutated amino acids. PrEMS serves as a quantitative framework to fill the knowledge gap in structural descriptors between sequence mutation and the enzyme's function, rationalizing enzyme improvement strategies. For example, our analysis indicated that photodamage can be suppressed by incorporating aromatic residues near the active site. Our study outlines a tangible path with quantifiable metrics for integrating native MS data into enzyme design workflows.
